Data

Database of vertebrate home range sizes. Reference: Tamburello N, Cote IM, Dulvy NK (2015) Energy and the scaling of animal space use. The American Naturalist 186(2):196-211. http://dx.doi.org/10.1086/682070.
Data: http://datadryad.org/resource/doi:10.5061/dryad.q5j65/1

1. Load the data into a new object called homerange.

homerange <- read.csv("data/Tamburelloetal_HomeRangeDatabase.csv")

2. What is the structure of the homerange data? Does it have any NA’s? Do a quick exploratory analysis of your choice below.

3. Which animal groups are represented in the data? Make a plot that shows the number in each class.

names(homerange)
##  [1] "taxon"                      "common.name"               
##  [3] "class"                      "order"                     
##  [5] "family"                     "genus"                     
##  [7] "species"                    "primarymethod"             
##  [9] "N"                          "mean.mass.g"               
## [11] "log10.mass"                 "alternative.mass.reference"
## [13] "mean.hra.m2"                "log10.hra"                 
## [15] "hra.reference"              "realm"                     
## [17] "thermoregulation"           "locomotion"                
## [19] "trophic.guild"              "dimension"                 
## [21] "preymass"                   "log10.preymass"            
## [23] "PPMR"                       "prey.size.reference"
ggplot(data = homerange,
      mapping = aes(x = class)) + 
      geom_bar(mapping = aes(fill = class)) +
      labs(title = "Number of Animal Groups in Each Class",
       x = "Class",
       y = "Number of Animal Groups")

4. Are there more carnivores or herbivores represented in the data? Make a plot that shows the number in each trophic guild.

ggplot(data = homerange,
      mapping = aes(x = trophic.guild)) + 
      geom_bar(mapping = aes(fill = trophic.guild)) +
      labs(title = "Number of Animal Groups in Each Trophic Guild",
       x = "Trophic Guild",
       y = "Number of Animal Groups")

There are more carnivores in the data than herbivores.

5. Which herbivorous mammals have homeranges greater than 1,000,000 m²? Show only the common name, order, mean homerange size, and mean body mass. Arrange the data in descending order by homerange size and show only the top 10 species.

homerange %>%
  select(common.name, order, mean.hra.m2, mean.mass.g) %>% 
  filter(mean.hra.m2 >= 1000000) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean.hra.m2)) %>%
  slice_max(mean.hra.m2, n = 10)
##              common.name         order mean.hra.m2 mean.mass.g
## 1               reindeer  artiodactyla  3550830977   102058.69
## 2  African bush elephant   proboscidea  1753759352  4000000.08
## 3           greater kudu  artiodactyla  1070039969   197314.95
## 4                cheetah     carnivora   815060788    50000.00
## 5                leopard     carnivora   504940261    48374.89
## 6                caracal     carnivora   376634414    12999.90
## 7              wolverine     carnivora   361917847    21545.67
## 8                 cougar     carnivora   312003884    89999.48
## 9         American bison  artiodactyla   265778594   629999.20
## 10              caracara falconiformes   241000000     1125.00

6. Which two species have the largest and smallest homerange sizes?

homerange %>%
  select(common.name, order, mean.hra.m2, mean.mass.g) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean.hra.m2)) %>%
  slice_max(mean.hra.m2, n = 1)
##   common.name        order mean.hra.m2 mean.mass.g
## 1    reindeer artiodactyla  3550830977    102058.7
homerange %>%
  select(common.name, order, mean.hra.m2, mean.mass.g) %>% 
  arrange(mean.hra.m2) %>%
  slice_min(mean.hra.m2, n = 1)
##   common.name       order mean.hra.m2 mean.mass.g
## 1  rusty goby perciformes        0.03        0.22

7. Which carnivorous mammals have the largest homeranges?

homerange %>%
  select(common.name, order, mean.hra.m2, mean.mass.g, trophic.guild) %>% 
  filter(trophic.guild == "carnivore") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean.hra.m2)) %>%
  slice_max(mean.hra.m2, n = 10)

8. Is there a relationship between body mass and homerange size? Make a scatterplot to show this relationship. Be sure to include appropriate labels and a title.

ggplot(data = homerange,
      mapping = aes(x = mean.mass.g,y = mean.hra.m2)) + 
      geom_point(mapping = aes(color = trophic.guild)) + 
      geom_smooth(method = lm, se = F, na.rm = T) +
      scale_x_log10() +
      scale_y_log10() + 
      labs(title = "Body Mass (g) vs. Homerange Size (m^2)",
       x = "Body Mass (g)",
       y = "Homerange Size (m^2)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

There is a relationship between body mass and homerange size.

9. Use filter to extract the data for only birds and mammals. Then make a plot that compares the homerange sizes of these two groups. Be sure to include appropriate labels and a title.

homerangebm = filter(homerange, taxon == "birds" | taxon == "mammals")

ggplot(data = homerangebm,
      mapping = aes(x = taxon, y = mean.hra.m2)) + 
      geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(fill = taxon)) +
      scale_y_log10() + 
      labs(title = "Taxon vs. Mean Homerange Size (m^2)",
       x = "Taxon",
       y = "Mean Homerange Size (m^2)")

10. Do one additional exploratory analysis of your choice. Before writing the code, write the question you are trying to answer. The question should be biologically meaningful and appropriate for the data. It must include at least one filter(), select(), and arrange(). The question I am trying to answer is out of all of the bird species in the data, do carnivores have a larger homerange size than herbivores?

homerange %>%
  select(common.name, taxon, order, family, trophic.guild, mean.mass.g, mean.hra.m2) %>% 
  filter(taxon == "birds") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean.hra.m2)) %>%
  slice_max(mean.hra.m2, n = 10)
##               common.name taxon            order        family trophic.guild
## 1                caracara birds    falconiformes    falconidae     carnivore
## 2       Montagu's harrier birds    falconiformes  accipitridae     carnivore
## 3        peregrine falcon birds    falconiformes    falconidae     carnivore
## 4            booted eagle birds  accipitriformes  accipitridae     carnivore
## 5                 ostrich birds struthioniformes struthionidae     herbivore
## 6  short-toed snake eagle birds  accipitriformes  accipitridae     carnivore
## 7    European turtle dove birds    columbiformes    columbidae     herbivore
## 8        Egyptian vulture birds  accipitriformes  accipitridae     carnivore
## 9          common buzzard birds  accipitriformes  accipitridae     carnivore
## 10          lanner falcon birds    falconiformes    falconidae     carnivore
##    mean.mass.g mean.hra.m2
## 1      1125.00   241000000
## 2       315.50   200980000
## 3       781.50   153860000
## 4       975.00   117300000
## 5     88250.00    84300000
## 6      1699.00    78500000
## 7       140.33    63585000
## 8      2203.00    63570000
## 9       846.00    50240000
## 10      675.00    50000000
homerangeb = filter(homerange, taxon == "birds")
ggplot(data = homerangeb,
      mapping = aes(x = trophic.guild, y = mean.hra.m2)) + 
      geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(fill = trophic.guild)) +
      scale_y_log10() + 
      labs(title = "Trophic Guild vs. Mean Homerange Size (m^2)",
       x = "Trophic Guild",
       y = "Mean Homerange Size (m^2)")
